meta.titre: Enthalpy Changes: Definitions, Hess's Law and Born-Haber Cycles
meta.sous_theme: Standard enthalpy changes and Hess's law

sections.contenu_markdown: A gas cylinder from the depot in Douala costs a few thousand FCFA and releases the heat of burning propane or butane, whereas a cold pack from a pharmacy gets cold when its salt dissolves. Both are enthalpy changes, the heat exchanged at constant pressure, and chemists use them to compare fuels, to predict which reactions will run and to calculate energies that cannot be measured directly. Every A Level paper contains at least a Hess's law cycle, a definition of a standard enthalpy change and a lattice-energy calculation, so the exact wording of each definition earns marks.

items: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings and has a negative enthalpy change; an endothermic reaction absorbs heat and has a positive one.
Amounts of substance are found with $n = m/M$ and the coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios.
The specific heat capacity of water is $4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and 1 g of dilute aqueous solution occupies about 1 $\mathrm{cm^{3}}$.
Ionic compounds are made of oppositely charged ions held in a giant lattice.

sections.titre: Definitions of enthalpy changes and Hess's law
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Standard conditions** are a pressure of 100 kPa, a stated temperature (usually 298 K) and every substance in its standard state. The symbol $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ means a standard enthalpy change, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

| Enthalpy change | Definition | Sign |
|---|---|---|
| Formation, $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ | one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, e.g. $\mathrm{Na(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$ | usually negative |
| Combustion, $\Delta H_c^{\ominus}$ | one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen | always negative |
| Atomisation, $\Delta H_{at}^{\ominus}$ | one mole of gaseous atoms forms from the element in its standard state, e.g. $\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na(g)}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl(g)}$ | positive |
| Neutralisation | one mole of water forms from an acid and a base, e.g. $\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$ | negative |
| First ionisation | $\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + e^{-}$ | positive |
| First electron affinity | one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons: $\mathrm{Cl(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}$ | usually negative |
| Hydration of an ion | gaseous ions dissolve in water: $\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(aq)}$ | always negative |
| Lattice enthalpy (formation) | gaseous ions form one mole of solid: $\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$ | always negative |

The second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic, $\mathrm{O^{-}(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{O^{2-}(g)}$ because an electron is forced onto an already negative ion, whereas the first, $\mathrm{O(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{O^{-}(g)}$ is exothermic.

**Hess's law.** The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whichever route is taken, provided the initial and final states are the same. From formation data: $\Delta H_r^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$. From combustion data the order is reversed: $\Delta H_r^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta H_c^{\ominus}(\text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta H_c^{\ominus}(\text{products})$. Multiply each value by its coefficient, keep the signs, and write every equation with state symbols.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid must be found from formation, atomisation, ionisation and electron affinity data.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to the formation of an ionic solid. For sodium chloride the route from the elements to the solid has these steps (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$):

- atomisation of sodium, $\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na(g)}$ : $+107$
- atomisation of chlorine, $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl(g)}$ : $+122$
- first ionisation of sodium, $\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + e^{-}$ : $+496$
- electron affinity of chlorine, $\mathrm{Cl(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}$ : $-349$
- lattice enthalpy, $\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$ : $\Delta H_L$
- the direct route, $\mathrm{Na(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$ : $-411$

Both routes link the same start and end, so $-411 = 107 + 122 + 496 - 349 + \Delta H_L$ and $\Delta H_L = -411 - 376 = -787\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. In this course lattice enthalpy is defined as the formation of the lattice from gaseous ions, so it is negative. Some textbooks define it as the reverse process and give a positive value, so read the definition in the question. A lattice enthalpy is larger in magnitude when ions are smaller and more highly charged. The enthalpy of solution is $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_L + \Delta H_{hyd}(\text{cation}) + \Delta H_{hyd}(\text{anion})$ with this sign convention.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When temperature changes in an experiment are used to find an enthalpy change.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The heat absorbed by the solution is $q = mc\Delta T$ with $c = 4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $m$ the mass of solution in grams. Then $\Delta H = -\dfrac{q}{n}$, where $n$ is the amount of the limiting reagent in moles. The minus sign makes a temperature rise correspond to a negative $\Delta H$. Convert $q$ from joules to kilojoules before quoting the answer. Heat loss to the surroundings makes the measured temperature rise too small, so the experimental enthalpy change is less exothermic than the true value.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a reaction is entirely in the gas phase and bond enthalpy values are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in gaseous molecules; it is positive. $\Delta H_r = \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed})$. For $\mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl(g)}$ the bond enthalpies are H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242 and H-Cl 431 $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$: $\Delta H = (436 + 242) - 2\times431 = -184\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Because the values are averages over many compounds, results are approximate.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The standard enthalpy changes of combustion at 298 K are: carbon (graphite) $-394\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, hydrogen $-286\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and propane gas $-2220\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Water is formed as a liquid in each case. ($\mathrm{C} = 12.0$, $\mathrm{H} = 1.0$.)

(a) Calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$, from these data.

(b) Calculate the heat released when 4.4 g of propane burns completely.

etapes.action: Write the equation that defines the quantity required.
etapes.justification: The enthalpy of formation is for one mole of the compound from its elements in their standard states.

etapes.action: Write the combustion equation of each substance.
etapes.justification: The data are combustion values, so each substance must be linked to the same products, carbon dioxide and liquid water.

Burning the elements gives the same products as burning propane, so the formation enthalpy is the difference between the two routes. Carbon is multiplied by 3 and hydrogen by 4 to match the coefficients of the formation equation.

etapes.action: Substitute the values and keep the signs.
etapes.justification: Each combustion value carries its own sign.

etapes.action: Find the heat for 4.4 g of propane.
etapes.justification: $M(\mathrm{C_3H_8}) = 3\times12.0 + 8\times1.0 = 44.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, so $n = 4.4/44.0 = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$ and the combustion enthalpy is per mole.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The standard enthalpy change of formation of propane is $-106\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and 4.4 g of propane releases 222 kJ on combustion.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing the formation of propane as $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}(g)} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{C(s)} + 4\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$ and giving $-106$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The formation equation must start from the elements in their standard states and form the compound. The reverse reaction has the opposite sign, so $+106$.

items.erreur_markdown: Using $\Delta H_r = \sum \Delta H_c(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_c(\text{reactants})$ with combustion data.
items.pourquoi_faux: With combustion data the reactants are burnt to the products, so the order is reversed compared with formation data.

items.erreur_markdown: Forgetting to multiply each enthalpy by its coefficient, for example using $-394$ instead of $3\times(-394)$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Enthalpy is an extensive quantity: three moles of carbon release three times the heat of one.
items.correction_markdown: Always multiply by the coefficient in the equation, then add the signed values.

items.erreur_markdown: In calorimetry, writing $\Delta H = +q/n$ for a reaction that warms the solution, or leaving $q$ in joules and $\Delta H$ in kJ.
items.pourquoi_faux: A temperature rise means heat leaves the reacting system, so $\Delta H$ is negative, and the units must match.
items.correction_markdown: $\Delta H = -\dfrac{q}{n}$, and convert joules to kilojoules by dividing by 1000.

items.erreur_markdown: "The lattice enthalpy of sodium chloride is positive because the lattice is stable." (with the formation definition)
items.pourquoi_faux: Stability comes from energy released when the ions come together. With the definition used here, the formation of a lattice from gaseous ions is exothermic.
items.correction_markdown: $\Delta H_L = -787\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for the formation of NaCl(s) from gaseous ions.

items.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment, 50.0 $\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ hydrochloric acid are mixed with 50.0 $\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ sodium hydroxide in an insulated cup. Both solutions start at the same temperature, and the temperature rises by 6.8 K. Assume the density of the mixture is $1.00\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and its specific heat capacity is $4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation per mole of water formed.
items.solution_markdown:
$m = 100\ \mathrm{g}$, so $q = mc\Delta T = 100\times4.18\times6.8 = 2842.4\ \mathrm{J}$.

$n(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 0.0500\ \mathrm{dm^3}\times1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$ (acid and alkali react 1 : 1).

$\Delta H = -\dfrac{2842.4}{0.0500} = -56\,848\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}} = \mathbf{-56.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}}$ (to 3 s.f.). The reaction is $\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$

items.enonce_markdown:
The standard enthalpy changes of combustion of ethene gas and of liquid ethanol are $-1411\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $-1367\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively.

(a) Write the equation for the combustion of one mole of ethanol.

(b) Use the data to calculate the enthalpy change for $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}(g)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}$ (Water does not burn.)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)} + 3\mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$

(b) Ethene burns to $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ and liquid water, and so does ethanol, so Hess's law with combustion data applies: $\Delta H = \sum \Delta H_c(\text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta H_c(\text{products}) = (-1411 + 0) - (-1367) = \mathbf{-44\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}}$. Liquid water is already a combustion product, so its value is zero.

items.enonce_markdown:
Use the following data, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, to find the lattice enthalpy of magnesium chloride (formation of the solid from gaseous ions). Enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$(s) $= -641$; atomisation of Mg $= +148$; first ionisation of Mg $= +738$; second ionisation of Mg $= +1451$; atomisation of chlorine, per mole of Cl atoms, $= +122$; first electron affinity of Cl $= -349$.

(a) Write the equation for the lattice enthalpy of magnesium chloride.

(b) Calculate its value.

(c) The lattice enthalpy of sodium chloride is $-787\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Explain why the value for magnesium chloride is much larger in magnitude.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}(g)} + 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}(s)}$

(b) The cycle needs two chlorine atoms and two electrons per formula unit: $\Delta H_f = \Delta H_{at}(\mathrm{Mg}) + IE_1 + IE_2 + 2\Delta H_{at}(\mathrm{Cl}) + 2EA_1 + \Delta H_L$. The sum of the other terms is $148 + 738 + 1451 + 2(122) + 2(-349) = 1883$. Hence $\Delta H_L = -641 - 1883 = \mathbf{-2524\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}}$.

(c) The magnesium ion has a 2+ charge and is smaller than the sodium ion, so its charge density is higher. The attraction between $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions is much stronger, and two chloride ions are attracted per magnesium ion, so more energy is released when the lattice forms.

items_markdown: A standard enthalpy change refers to 100 kPa, a stated temperature (usually 298 K) and standard states; quote the unit $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and learn each definition word for word.
Formation is for one mole of compound from its elements; combustion is for one mole of substance burnt completely in oxygen and is always negative.
Hess's law: with formation data, products minus reactants; with combustion data, reactants minus products; multiply by coefficients and keep signs.
A Born-Haber cycle gives the lattice enthalpy: $\Delta H_f = \Delta H_{at} + IE + EA + \Delta H_{L}$ summed over every step; lattice enthalpy is larger for smaller, more highly charged ions.
Calorimetry: $q = mc\Delta T$ and $\Delta H = -q/n$, with $q$ converted to kJ.
The first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic, the second endothermic; hydration of gaseous ions is always exothermic.
